_meta.description: Thresholds and weights that map commodity properties to desirable packaging material properties. Consumed by backend/engine/recommender.py. These are simplified heuristics for a rules-based prototype, not a substitute for actual shelf-life/migration testing.

oxygen_sensitive_categories._note: Categories that need a materially tighter O2 barrier for reasons OTHER than fat oxidation (the only thing high_fat_percent captures) — aroma retention for ground spices, and raw-protein freshness/color/microbial safety for meat & fish. Without this, the oxygen-fit rule only ever tightened for high-fat commodities, so a cheap low-barrier material like HDPE could win on cost+category despite being unsuitable for a spice pouch or raw meat pack. Caught by evaluation/run_evaluation.py after fixing the category-taxonomy bug exposed the gap underneath it.

moisture_sensitive_categories._note: Categories where a commodity NOT already caught by the high_moisture_percent branch below (i.e. a dried/cured/intermediate-moisture product, not a fresh wet one) still needs a tight moisture barrier for a reason other than generic staleness: moisture re-uptake in a previously dehydration/salt-preserved protein risks enabling microbial regrowth — a food-safety-adjacent failure mode, not just a quality one. Without this, a commodity like dried salted fish (~20% moisture — dried enough to be 'preserved', but not dry enough to trip low_moisture_percent) fell through to the lenient default_max_wvtr target meant for genuinely moderate-moisture goods like bread or cheese, letting a merely-adequate barrier (e.g. compostable film) tie with a purpose-built barrier laminate on every other dimension and win narrowly on sustainability alone. Uses high_moisture_commodity_max_wvtr as the target (reusing the existing 'meat needs a tight barrier' number rather than inventing a new one) — fresh, wet items in this category already get that same target via the moisture_mid >= high_moisture_percent branch, so this only affects the dried/cured middle band. Caught investigating dried_fish's top pick after the 80-commodity dataset expansion; see evaluation/reference_cases.py's dried_fish_default case.

respiration_class_packaging_boost._note: Explicit scoring bonus — separate from the numeric respiration_otr_bands check below — for materials tagged breathable=true in packaging_materials.json, applied when the commodity's respiration_rate_class is in 'classes'. Needed because a material can land inside the respiration_otr_bands range purely by coincidence of its own bulk resin permeability (e.g. plain LDPE is naturally permeable) without actually being a vented/perforated product engineered for produce airflow. Without this, cheap incidentally-permeable resins could outrank purpose-built breathable materials on cost/category/sustainability alone. Added after evaluation/run_evaluation.py showed strawberry and spinach (both very_high respiration) consistently NOT getting a breathable-tagged top pick.

category_preferred_material_categories._note: A commodity's preferred list should include every material category tag that can physically take a flexible/rigid form matching that preference — e.g. 'flexible_film_or_rigid' and 'rigid_or_film' materials (HDPE, PP, PET) are legitimate flexible-film choices too, not just materials tagged exactly 'flexible_film'. Omitting those caused a taxonomy bug: cheap, common produce-bag materials (HDPE/PP) were losing category credit to a pricier niche material purely from a string mismatch, not an actual property difference. Caught by evaluation/run_evaluation.py.

packaging_format_practicality._note: Genuine physical-format factor, separate from barrier performance and cost tier: how practical a material's typical packaging FORMAT is for high-volume retail distribution — weight, breakage/fragility risk in transport, and pallet/shelf density. This exists because zero-permeability materials (glass) were maxing the moisture/oxygen scores and, once their sustainability score was also high, nothing meaningfully weighed against them for everyday retail goods (cheese, butter, biscuits, cake) where a flexible film or laminate with comparable practical barrier performance is the actual industry norm — cost tier alone wasn't a strong enough counterweight. This is not 'penalize glass'; every material is scored on the same practicality question, glass simply scores low on it for a real, stated reason (heavy + fragile + low pallet density), and remains free to win on other dimensions when a rigid, zero-permeability format is genuinely decisive (e.g. very acidic or high-fat products where its barrier is precisely the point) or cost/practicality is de-prioritized (premium tier). Caught by evaluation/run_evaluation.py's Day 3 dairy/bakery mismatches. Scores are 0-10; converted to a 0-1 fraction the same way sustainability points are.

map_gas_guidance_by_respiration_class._note: General, commonly-documented MAP starting-point ranges grouped by respiration rate class — not commodity-specific lab-tested values. N2 is computed as the balance (100 - O2 - CO2), not stored directly.

packaging_weight_g_per_kg_product_by_cat._note: Rough, CATEGORY-level estimate of how many grams of packaging material are typically used per kg of commodity packaged — e.g. a small retail spice pouch uses proportionally far more material per kg of product than a bulk grain sack, purely from surface-area-to-weight geometry, independent of which material is chosen. Used ONLY to compute the informational estimated_cost_per_unit_inr figure in /recommend/detailed (see engine/recommender.py's _estimate_packaging_cost_per_unit) — this table is NOT read anywhere in the scoring/ranking path (_score_material), and budget_tier's existing directional influence on ranking is completely unaffected by it. This table is deliberately per-CATEGORY only (surface-area-to-weight geometry of the PRODUCT), not per-material — format/density differences BETWEEN materials (e.g. a glass jar genuinely using more grams than a thin film for the same product) are handled separately, by packaging_materials.json's material_weight_multiplier, applied on top of this table's figure in the same calculation. Even with that correction, both inputs are rough directional estimates, not precise engineering data — treat the resulting cost figures as directional planning estimates, not quotes.

logistics._note: Converts a haversine (straight-line) distance in km into a rough estimated transport-days figure for the /logistics/estimate-transport-days endpoint (engine/logistics.py). km_per_transport_day models DIRECT ROAD FREIGHT transit time — a loaded truck actually moving city-to-city on Indian highways (accounting for loading/unloading, rest stops, checkposts, and the fact that road distance runs longer than straight-line distance) — NOT last-mile farm-to-mandi collection speed, which is far slower and not what this endpoint estimates. 350 km/day reflects typical direct road-freight timing (e.g. Mumbai-Delhi's ~1150 km straight-line distance lands around 3-4 days, matching real-world freight schedules for that route). If this constant is ever revisited, keep it anchored to direct road-freight speed, not collection/last-mile logistics — conflating the two previously produced wildly unrealistic day-counts (e.g. 25+ days for Mumbai-Delhi). min_transport_days is a floor so two nearby cities don't round to 0 days, which would be misleading (loading/handling alone takes time even for a short hop). This is explicitly a rough planning estimate, not a routed ETA — see the endpoint's disclaimer field.
